patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] mm/hmm: reject shadow-stack mappings
patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch rejects shadow-stack mappings in the Heterogeneous Memory Management (HMM) module to prevent devices from gaining write access to user-space shadow stacks on x86 architectures.

review_comments.author: Lorenzo (ARM)
review_comments.summary: Reviewer noted that the patch does not explicitly check for shadow stacks in hmm_vma_walk_test() and requested a check be added to prevent devices from gaining write access to shadow stacks.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Fri, Nov 13, 2026 at 02:55:36PM -0500, Gregory Price (Meta) wrote:
> HMM can grant ordinary device write access to a userspace shadow stack.
> On x86, pte_write() is true for a shadow-stack PTE, so a populated page
> can be returned with HMM_PFN_WRITE without taking a CPU write fault.
>
> Nouveau translates that flag into a writable GPU mapping.
>
> Reject shadow-stack VMAs in hmm_vma_walk_test(). Use the existing
> unsupported-range handling: a requested fault returns -EFAULT, while a
> snapshot records HMM_PFN_ERROR.
>
> Link: https://lore.kernel.org/linux-mm/20261111-mason-migrate-et-al-fixes-v1-10-3d2454362e8d@kernel.org/
> Fixes: 54007f818206 ("mm: Introduce VM_SHADOW_STACK for shadow stack memory")
> Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
> Cc: "Lorenzo Stoakes (ARM)" <ljs@kernel.org>
> Signed-off-by: Gregory Price (Meta) <gourry@gourry.net>

Thanks for doing the HMM side of this, LGTM and:

Reviewed-by: Lorenzo Stoakes (ARM) <ljs@kernel.org>

> ---
>  mm/hmm.c | 3 +++
>  1 file changed, 3 insertions(+)
>
> diff --git a/mm/hmm.c b/mm/hmm.c
> index 2f1e98c6b644..fa61ca59d927 100644
> --- a/mm/hmm.c
> +++ b/mm/hmm.c
> @@ -596,6 +596,7 @@ static int hmm_vma_walk_test(unsigned long start, unsigned long end,
>  	struct vm_area_struct *vma = walk->vma;
>
>  	if (!(vma->vm_flags & (VM_IO | VM_PFNMAP)) &&
> +	    !vma_test_single_mask(vma, VMA_SHADOW_STACK) &&
>  	    vma->vm_flags & VM_READ)
>  		return 0;
>
> @@ -607,6 +608,8 @@ static int hmm_vma_walk_test(unsigned long start, unsigned long end,
>  	 * allow write access either. HMM does not support architectures that
>  	 * allow write without read.
>  	 *
> +	 * Devices must not gain ordinary write access to shadow stacks.
> +	 *
>  	 * If a fault is requested for an unsupported range then it is a hard
>  	 * failure.
>  	 */
> --
> 2.56.0
>

--
Cheers, Lorenzo

On 11/14/26 08:25, Gregory Price (Meta) wrote:
> On 2026-11-13 20:20 -0400, Jason Gunthorpe wrote:
>> On Fri, Nov 13, 2026 at 03:41:33PM -0500, Gregory Price (Meta) wrote:
>>>
>>> Some of the context is here:
>>> https://lore.kernel.org/all/20261111-mason-migrate-et-al-fixes-v1-10-3d2454362e8d@kernel.org/
>>>
>>> We had a similar issue with migration, but this should handle the DMA
>>> case as well.
>>>
>>> It's "technically writable" but the kernel is supposed to prevent that.
>>
>> Bah, it's not writable at all. The CPU PTE has write disabled and
>> someone thought it was a good idea to make pte_write() return true
>> because the CPU allows writes through a special instruction on this
>> special PTE? So now all the places like this think its writable, when
>> it really isn't.
>>
> 
> I completely missed this, that will teach me to trust pte_write() I
> guess... what a bizarre design choice.  I'm sure there's "reasons".
> 
>> You could also fix this by having something like pte_real_write() or
>> whatever that doesn't lie about the write bit in the PTE :|
>>
> 
> or rename pte_write() to pte_fake_write() instead and restore
> pte_write() to its former truthful glory

It's writable by the hardware, that's what matters to core-mm, for example, when
it comes to things like fork(), mproetect() etc.

*nobody* besides selected core-mm code should ever write to random PTEs. They
shouldn't ever even care about pte_write().

We have GUP for that, which takes care of that oddity properly when deciding
whether we can *actually* write to a mapped page.

Well, and we have HMM that reimplements part of GUP in ugly ways (sorry) that we
missed.

-- 
Cheers,

David

On 11/19/26 21:05, Dave Hansen wrote:
> On 11/14/26 17:01, Andrew Morton wrote:
>> On x86, a shadow-stack PTE has its ordinary write bit clear.  The CPU
>> rejects ordinary stores, but pte_write() reports it writable because
>> shadow-stack instructions can write it.  HMM consequently sets
>> HMM_PFN_WRITE.  Nouveau uses that flag for GPU write permission, and
>> RDMA on-demand paging can use it to grant device write permission to a
>> registered memory region.  A device, or an RDMA peer with write access
>> to that region, can then overwrite the process's shadow stack,
>> potentially corrupting return addresses or bypassing that protection.
>>
>> Reject shadow-stack VMAs in hmm_vma_walk_test(), including read access.
>> A requested fault returns -EFAULT; a snapshot records HMM_PFN_ERROR.
> 
> This is a fun one.
> 
> I almost wonder if we want to go one step further and disallow GUPs with
> FOLL_WRITE on these PTEs. There should be precious few reasons for
> devices to be writing to shadow stack pages.
> 
> Isn't this a bigger issue than HMM? Should the fix be in HMM?

I think we discussed this excessively after I raised it and it's even partially
documented in the relevant commit messages.

-- 
Cheers,

David

On 11/19/26 21:40, Edgecombe, Rick P wrote:
> On Thu, 2026-11-19 at 12:05 -0800, Dave Hansen wrote:
>> On 11/14/26 17:01, Andrew Morton wrote:
>>> On x86, a shadow-stack PTE has its ordinary write bit clear. The CPU
>>> rejects ordinary stores, but pte_write() reports it writable because
>>> shadow-stack instructions can write it. HMM consequently sets
>>> HMM_PFN_WRITE. Nouveau uses that flag for GPU write permission, and
>>> RDMA on-demand paging can use it to grant device write permission to a
>>> registered memory region. A device, or an RDMA peer with write access
>>> to that region, can then overwrite the process's shadow stack,
>>> potentially corrupting return addresses or bypassing that protection.
>>>
>>> Reject shadow-stack VMAs in hmm_vma_walk_test(), including read access.
>>> A requested fault returns -EFAULT; a snapshot records HMM_PFN_ERROR.
>>
>> This is a fun one.
>>
>> I almost wonder if we want to go one step further and disallow GUPs with
>> FOLL_WRITE on these PTEs. There should be precious few reasons for
>> devices to be writing to shadow stack pages.
>>
>> Isn't this a bigger issue than HMM? Should the fix be in HMM?
> 
> We do reject GUPs to shadow stack PTEs with FOLL_WRITE, unless FOLL_FORCE is
> passed. The tricky thing as mentioned my others in this thread is that shadow
> stack memory *is* writable by userspace. But also the kernel should not treat it
> as such
> 
> A false negative for pte_write() is dangerous when the kernel needs to decide
> when to revoke access. (i.e. fork) I think a mistake there is somewhat worse
> then missing an exotic way to cajole the kernel into writing to a user's shadow
> stack like this. So I think pte_write() being true for shadow stacks is the
> correct implementation.
> 
> But, maybe the problem is that pte_write() is doing the job of two separate
> concepts. What if there was a pte_userspace_could_write() and a
> pte_kernel_should_not_write()? Names would need some work...

Gah, nak,

pte_write() just says "something might be able to write to it".

If that's actually true depends on other factors. Like the access+dirty on HW
that manages that in software.

I repeat: *no code* in Linux besides core-mm should ever interpret "pte_write()"
as "cool, I can write to it". The exception is GUP and unfortunately HMM.

-- 
Cheers,

David

review_comments.author: Jason Gunthorpe
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Jason Gunthorpe noted that the shadow-stack PTE has its ordinary write bit clear on x86, but pte_write() reports it writable because shadow-stack instructions can write to it; this allows HMM to set HMM_PFN_WRITE, which Nouveau and RDMA use for GPU and device write permission respectively, potentially allowing a device or RDMA peer to overwrite the process's shadow stack. He suggested adding details about this behavior in the patch description.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Fri, Nov 13, 2026 at 02:55:36PM -0500, Gregory Price (Meta) wrote:
> HMM can grant ordinary device write access to a userspace shadow stack.
> On x86, pte_write() is true for a shadow-stack PTE, so a populated page
> can be returned with HMM_PFN_WRITE without taking a CPU write fault.

I'm not sure I understand this? The pte is writable but you don't want
only DMA to write to it?

Is there something special on x86 that makes the shadow stack pte
non-writable by the CPU?

A few more words here would help

Regardless, this seems reasonable to me, there is no use case to
write to the shadow stack..

Reviewed-by: Jason Gunthorpe <jgg@nvidia.com>

Jason

> Some of the context is here:
> https://lore.kernel.org/all/20261111-mason-migrate-et-al-fixes-v1-10-3d2454362e8d@kernel.org/
> 
> We had a similar issue with migration, but this should handle the DMA
> case as well.
> 
> It's "technically writable" but the kernel is supposed to prevent that.

Bah, it's not writable at all. The CPU PTE has write disabled and
someone thought it was a good idea to make pte_write() return true
because the CPU allows writes through a special instruction on this
special PTE? So now all the places like this think its writable, when
it really isn't.

You could also fix this by having something like pte_real_write() or
whatever that doesn't lie about the write bit in the PTE :|

The patch is still fine, in that it matches what everything else does,
but I'd include these details someplace..

Jason

> > : shadow-stack instructions can write it.  HMM consequently sets
> > : HMM_PFN_WRITE, which Nouveau turns into ordinary GPU write permission.  A
> > : process with GPU access can then overwrite its own shadow stack,
> > : potentially corrupting return addresses or bypassing that protection.
> > : 
> > : Reject shadow-stack VMAs in hmm_vma_walk_test(), including read access.  A
> > : requested fault returns -EFAULT; a snapshot records HMM_PFN_ERROR.
> 
> Yes, but it is not just nouveau, RDMA user can do this too and
> that is far more common..

Thanks.  This?

On x86, a shadow-stack PTE has its ordinary write bit clear.  The CPU
rejects ordinary stores, but pte_write() reports it writable because
shadow-stack instructions can write it.  HMM consequently sets
HMM_PFN_WRITE.  Nouveau uses that flag for GPU write permission, and
RDMA on-demand paging can use it to grant device write permission to a
registered memory region.  A device, or an RDMA peer with write access
to that region, can then overwrite the process's shadow stack,
potentially corrupting return addresses or bypassing that protection.

Reject shadow-stack VMAs in hmm_vma_walk_test(), including read access.
A requested fault returns -EFAULT; a snapshot records HMM_PFN_ERROR.

review_comments.author: Alistair Popple
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Alistair Popple noted that pte_write() is documented to return true if a page is logically writable, which can lead to confusion and incorrect assumptions about PTE writeability. He pointed out that this issue was not universally applicable, as _PAGE_RW = 0, and suggested that the fix looks good.

> >>> case as well.

Yeah, I asked the HMM question there -
https://lore.kernel.org/linux-mm/avT2FNTZoEuijEZP@nvdebian.thelocal/

> >>>
> >>> It's "technically writable" but the kernel is supposed to prevent that.
> >>
> >> Bah, it's not writable at all. The CPU PTE has write disabled and
> >> someone thought it was a good idea to make pte_write() return true
> >> because the CPU allows writes through a special instruction on this
> >> special PTE? So now all the places like this think its writable, when
> >> it really isn't.
> >>
> > 
> > I completely missed this, that will teach me to trust pte_write() I
> > guess... what a bizarre design choice.  I'm sure there's "reasons".

Yeah, that surprised me as well when I looked into how the shadow stack worked.

> >> You could also fix this by having something like pte_real_write() or
> >> whatever that doesn't lie about the write bit in the PTE :|
> >>

Except they're not universally writable by HW, after all _PAGE_RW = 0. So
pte_write() is documented to return if it is logically writable, which of course
is what hmm_range_fault() also needs for certain values of "logic" :-)

So it's easy to see how this is confusing and got missed. Anyway this fix looks

> David

review_comments.author: Dave Hansen
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Dave Hansen noted that on x86, shadow-stack PTEs have their ordinary write bit clear, but pte_write() reports them writable due to shadow-stack instructions; this allows devices or RDMA peers to overwrite the process's shadow stack, potentially corrupting return addresses or bypassing protection. He suggested rejecting shadow-stack VMAs in hmm_vma_walk_test(), including read access, and also considered disallowing GUPs with FOLL_WRITE on these PTEs.
review_comments.raw_body:
On 11/14/26 17:01, Andrew Morton wrote:
> On x86, a shadow-stack PTE has its ordinary write bit clear.  The CPU
> rejects ordinary stores, but pte_write() reports it writable because
> shadow-stack instructions can write it.  HMM consequently sets
> HMM_PFN_WRITE.  Nouveau uses that flag for GPU write permission, and
> RDMA on-demand paging can use it to grant device write permission to a
> registered memory region.  A device, or an RDMA peer with write access
> to that region, can then overwrite the process's shadow stack,
> potentially corrupting return addresses or bypassing that protection.
> 
> Reject shadow-stack VMAs in hmm_vma_walk_test(), including read access.
> A requested fault returns -EFAULT; a snapshot records HMM_PFN_ERROR.

This is a fun one.

I almost wonder if we want to go one step further and disallow GUPs with
FOLL_WRITE on these PTEs. There should be precious few reasons for
devices to be writing to shadow stack pages.

Isn't this a bigger issue than HMM? Should the fix be in HMM?

review_comments.author: Edgecombe, P
review_comments.summary: Reviewer noted that shadow-stack PTEs have their ordinary write bit clear, but pte_write() reports them writable because shadow-stack instructions can write to them; this allows devices or RDMA peers with write access to overwrite the process's shadow stack, potentially corrupting return addresses or bypassing protection. The reviewer suggested rejecting shadow-stack VMAs in hmm_vma_walk_test(), including read access, and proposed considering a separate pte_userspace_could_write() function to handle user-space writable PTEs.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Sat, 2026-11-14 at 17:01 -0800, Andrew Morton wrote:
> Thanks.  This?
> 
> On x86, a shadow-stack PTE has its ordinary write bit clear.  The CPU
> rejects ordinary stores, but pte_write() reports it writable because
> shadow-stack instructions can write it.  HMM consequently sets
> HMM_PFN_WRITE.  Nouveau uses that flag for GPU write permission, and
> RDMA on-demand paging can use it to grant device write permission to a
> registered memory region.  A device, or an RDMA peer with write access
> to that region, can then overwrite the process's shadow stack,
> potentially corrupting return addresses or bypassing that protection.
> 
> Reject shadow-stack VMAs in hmm_vma_walk_test(), including read access.
> A requested fault returns -EFAULT; a snapshot records HMM_PFN_ERROR.

BTW, this is not just an x86 thing. Arm and riscv have the same pte_write()
shadow stack behavior for the same reasons. Despite not having the
Write=0,Dirty=1 thing, which *is* weird. But they still try to prevent the
kernel from writing it via logic in gup, etc.

---

On Thu, 2026-11-19 at 12:05 -0800, Dave Hansen wrote:
> On 11/14/26 17:01, Andrew Morton wrote:
> > On x86, a shadow-stack PTE has its ordinary write bit clear.  The CPU
> > rejects ordinary stores, but pte_write() reports it writable because
> > shadow-stack instructions can write it.  HMM consequently sets
> > HMM_PFN_WRITE.  Nouveau uses that flag for GPU write permission, and
> > RDMA on-demand paging can use it to grant device write permission to a
> > registered memory region.  A device, or an RDMA peer with write access
> > to that region, can then overwrite the process's shadow stack,
> > potentially corrupting return addresses or bypassing that protection.
> > 
> > Reject shadow-stack VMAs in hmm_vma_walk_test(), including read access.
> > A requested fault returns -EFAULT; a snapshot records HMM_PFN_ERROR.
> 
> This is a fun one.
> 
> I almost wonder if we want to go one step further and disallow GUPs with
> FOLL_WRITE on these PTEs. There should be precious few reasons for
> devices to be writing to shadow stack pages.
> 
> Isn't this a bigger issue than HMM? Should the fix be in HMM?

We do reject GUPs to shadow stack PTEs with FOLL_WRITE, unless FOLL_FORCE is
passed. The tricky thing as mentioned my others in this thread is that shadow
stack memory *is* writable by userspace. But also the kernel should not treat it
as such

A false negative for pte_write() is dangerous when the kernel needs to decide
when to revoke access. (i.e. fork) I think a mistake there is somewhat worse
then missing an exotic way to cajole the kernel into writing to a user's shadow
stack like this. So I think pte_write() being true for shadow stacks is the
correct implementation.

But, maybe the problem is that pte_write() is doing the job of two separate
concepts. What if there was a pte_userspace_could_write() and a
pte_kernel_should_not_write()? Names would need some work...

version_history.subject: [PATCH] NFSD: Reject a COPY whose source and destination are the same file

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses a requirement in RFC 7862 that the NFSD server must reject COPY operations where the source and destination files are the same, regardless of range overlap. The existing code only checks for overlapping ranges, which is also required by CLONE operations. The patch adds a check to nfsd4_setup_intra_ssc() to verify if the source and destination file handles refer to the same file.

review_comments.author: Chuck Lever
review_comments.summary: Identified the patch as a valid solution to the problem and applied it to nfsd-testing without any issues.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Thu, 19 Nov 2026 09:42:56 -0800, Jeff Layton wrote:
> RFC 7862 Section 15.2.3 says that COPY MUST fail with NFS4ERR_INVAL
> when SAVED_FH and CURRENT_FH refer to the same file, whatever the
> ranges. NFSD never checks for this. A same-file COPY with
> non-overlapping ranges succeeds, and one with overlapping ranges fails
> only because the VFS rejects it.
> 
> The overlap-only rule applies to CLONE (Section 15.13.3), so leave
> nfsd4_verify_copy() alone. Instead, check in nfsd4_setup_intra_ssc(),
> after both stateids are verified. For an inter-server copy, SAVED_FH
> names a file on another server, so that path is not affected.
> 
> [...]

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 1/4] mm: zswap: fix shrinker count for the root memcg
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the zswap shrinker, which incorrectly scales the number of freeable entries on a memcg's zswap LRU by the memcg's compression ratio for the root memcg. The issue arises from the fact that the root memcg's stats do not account for its own zswap entries, leading to incorrect scaling and potential data loss. To fix this, the patch uses the zswap pool-wide counters for the root memcg instead of relying on its local statistics.

review_comments.summary:
Author acknowledged that the root memcg's stats should include accounted kernel memory allocated by tasks in the root cgroup, but stated that addressing this is left for a separate subsequent patchset.

Author acknowledges that the analysis is correct and agrees to add NR_VMSCAN_WRITE to the allowlist, also plans to investigate adding more stats to the allowlist as suggested by Sashiko.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Chris,

Thanks for reviewing and testing this series!

---

I think your analysis is right. I'll add NR_VMSCAN_WRITE to the allow
list as well.

Sashiko pointed out that NR_SWAPCACHE and the other charged-folio
stats between WORKINGSET_RESTORE_FILE and
PGPROMOTE_SUCCESS in memcg_node_stat_items[] also should be added as
well. I need to look into this more.

I'm out on PTO for three weeks but when I come back, I'll update this
series and submit v4.

Thanks,
Joanne

review_comments.author: Joanne Koong (author)
review_comments.summary:
Author acknowledged that the root memcg's stats should include accounted kernel memory allocated by tasks in the root cgroup, and agreed to address this in a separate subsequent patchset.

The author is addressing Chris Down's feedback about adding a helper function for ratelimited flushes and non-ratelimited flushes, which Joanne found to be overkill after testing. Instead of implementing the helper, she suggests adding comments at the callsites and above lruvec_use_node_stat() to document the dependency.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Chris,

On Mon, Nov 16, 2026 at 9:07 PM Chris Down <chris@chrisdown.name> wrote:

---

Thanks for reviewing and testing this series. When I was updating v2
-> v3, I tested out what adding the helper looks like, but found it a
bit overkill. It adds two new api wrappers (one for ratelimited
flushes for workingset, and one for non-ratelimited flushes for
damon), each of which has only one callsite.

Maybe it would be clearest to add a comment directly at the callsites
and above lruvec_use_node_stat() to document the dependency? I'm happy
to add this in, or if you and Michal prefer the helper still, I'm
happy to add the helper APIs.

Thanks,
Joanne
